**Trigger firing**: Both variants triggered the expected behavior 100% of the time across all evals — this dimension shows no difference and isn't informative here.

**Expected output / overall correctness**: Both variants struggled heavily to meet the full expected output across most evals, typically scoring 0/3 on strict expected-output criteria (e.g., ecr-guard-gap-h1-exact-list, h2-safe-to-leave, account-sweep, draft-policy-preview, production-tag-catch-all, unexpected-deletion-postmortem, evaluation-five-rule-expiry-list). This indicates the underlying behavior/report format itself is not being fully satisfied by either variant in most scenarios — a shared weakness rather than a point of differentiation. In the few evals where a difference emerged: "evaluation-v230-in-use" favored without_skill slightly (1/3 vs 0/3), "evaluation-push-correlated-event-excluded" favored with_skill (3/3 vs 2/3), and "evaluation-cloudtrail-consumer-pull-in-use" favored with_skill (2/3 vs 0/3). These are mixed and eval-specific, not a consistent pattern.

**Per-assertion detail**: Within nearly every eval, several assertions always pass for both variants (e.g., "no write API called," certain tag/image listing checks) and several always fail for both (e.g., report heading structure, Check Matrix formatting, SIMULATED/AUTHORITATIVE labeling, Repository Rating vocabulary) — these shared failures point to gaps in the expected behavior itself rather than a variant-specific issue. Many assertions are flagged "flaky," passing inconsistently across the 3 runs for one or both variants, suggesting run-to-run variability rather than a stable capability gap. A smaller number of assertions clearly differentiate the variants: in "ecr-guard-gap-h1-exact-list," with_skill passed two assertions (AUTHORITATIVE/SIMULATED labeling, StartLifecyclePolicyPreview handling) that without_skill always failed. In "unexpected-deletion-postmortem," with_skill mentioned PolicyExecutionEvent while without_skill did not. Aggregate assertion pass rates per eval show with_skill at or above without_skill in most evals (e.g., 39% vs 18%, 19% vs 15%, 33% vs 25%, 57%→67% split, 60% vs 37%, 67% vs 47%), with a couple of near-ties (46% vs 41%, 14% vs 14%, 19% vs 17%).

**Runtime and cost**: Variant_a was consistently and often substantially faster and cheaper than with_skill across every eval where both ran (e.g., 2m40s/$1.33 vs 4m20s/$2.16; 31s/$0.26 vs 1m49s/$0.91; 44s/$0.37 vs 3m44s/$1.87; several cases where without_skill's measured runtime/cost rounded to 0s/$0.00, suggesting those runs were cached, skipped-compute, or not separately metered). This is a sizeable and consistent pattern in favor of without_skill's efficiency, but it runs alongside with_skill generally showing equal-or-better assertion pass rates, so this is a cost/thoroughness tradeoff rather than a clear win for either side.

**Output consistency across repeated runs**: Mixed and generally weak for both variants. Variant_b was rated "consistent" in one eval, "mostly_consistent" in several, but "inconsistent" in a couple (e.g., gap-h1-exact-list, evaluation-five-rule-expiry-list, evaluation-cloudtrail-consumer-pull-in-use). Variant_a was mostly "mostly_consistent" with one "inconsistent" rating. Several evals have no consistency data (null) for one or both variants, limiting how much can be concluded here.

**Quality comparison pairs**: For nearly all evals, 0 quality pairs were evaluated (skipped), meaning head-to-head quality judgments are largely unavailable. The one eval with quality data ("push-correlated-event-excluded") showed a split: without_skill favored on accuracy (2/2), with_skill favored on actionability (1/1 with 1 comparable), and completeness tied (comparable in both cases) — a small, mixed sample (only 2 pairs evaluated) that shouldn't be over-weighted.

**Confidence caveats**: Most expected-output and assertion judgments carry "high" or "medium" avg_confidence, lending reasonable weight to the findings, though several individual assertions (e.g., pull-window verdict, AccessDenied handling) are rated "low" confidence, and the quality-comparison sample size is very small (2-3 pairs) where present at all.

**Overall picture**: Neither variant reliably meets the strict expected-output bar on this report-generation task; a substantial share of assertions fail for both variants, pointing to a common underlying gap in behavior rather than a variant-specific deficiency. Where variants differ, with_skill somewhat more often passes additional assertions (particularly around labeling simulated/authoritative results and some evidence citations) and shows better aggregate assertion rates in most evals, while without_skill is consistently much faster and cheaper to run. Consistency across repeated runs is moderate and mixed for both.
